sets.notes: Exact BSB quotes and careful, text-only claims throughout, like quoting "but Ruth clung to her" for card 20. It's flat with almost no laughs, slips a food-rule line ("Keep your eyes on the bread" when the text says food), and repeats stiff phrasing like "The text says it is True."

Faithful, warm and well-sized, with care on heavy cards and a nice textual catch ("That little word 'but' tells you the two of them part ways"). It reuses the Prep line "I think this one hurts" word for word, and the humor rarely gets past pleasant.

It has real comic energy at times, like the "Burnt Batch" rename bit for Mara. It breaks hard rules (a joke that the names sound "like someone clearing their throat", "Wheat's wrong.") and piles on unreferenced extras like Joseph's grain, "house of bread" and Edom being "east of Israel."

It's lively and varied, with decent comparisons like "not waiting around for a postcard." It includes code reactions ("Box-worthy answer, baker!", "Fine work, baker!"), invents details like "penniless widow", "weathered face" and "brought bread back to Bethlehem", and adds unsourced facts like Naomi meaning 'pleasant' and the autumn olive harvest.

It mostly stays close to the verses with plain wording. Nearly every explanation is only one or two sentences, it adds stray facts like "kings sitting in Jerusalem", and there's no Papa Dorin personality or address to the baker.

Its facts track the verses closely and it never overreaches. It opens many explanations with code reactions ("Perfect bake!", "Box-worthy!", "Baked just right!"), and lines like "That is the word the text uses" read robotic.
It's thorough and cites verses consistently. It uses em dashes repeatedly, calls answers "wrong" and "incorrect", adds theology ("in God's providence"), and sounds like a commentary, not Papa Dorin.

Exact BSB quotes and solid true/false handling, like the full-and-empty reversal on card 13. It adds facts and reasons the text doesn't give ("east of the Dead Sea", "Moab was the destination because that is where they could find food", barley meaning "early spring"), and the formal no-contraction voice has no humor.

It's clear and mostly accurate on the core answers. Most explanations are under three sentences and end with bare references like "Ruth 1:13.", and it adds claims like Edom being where "food might be easier to find" and the townswomen being "shocked by how she's changed."
